title: The long way from
concrete to code.
intro.lede: I’m Razeen, a data engineer and AI solutions engineer in Malaysia who started out as a civil engineer. I build systems, test ideas in public repos, and run long distances to keep my head straight.
intro.note: Told step by step and kept as a journal, so it grows as I do.
body: This page is the longer version of that sentence: how a civil engineer ended up building data platforms and AI tools, the loop I use for all of it, and what happens away from the screen.

chapters.title: Engineer by training
body: Civil Engineering at Universiti Putra Malaysia: four years of structures, soils and calculations that had to be right the first time. I registered as a Graduate Engineer with the Board of Engineers Malaysia and the Institution of Engineers Malaysia, and joined G&P Geotechnic. The engineering was real. So was the pile of repetitive work around it.

chapters.title: Automating the boring parts
body: I taught myself Python and VBA to do the repetitive parts of geotechnical analysis, and realised I cared more about the data than the drawings. I studied at night for the Certified Data Analyst Associate, PCEP and Power BI certifications, then left engineering for a Data Analyst role at EISmartwork, building models on more than ten million records and dashboards people actually used.

chapters.title: Going deeper
body: Analytics made me want to understand the models, not just use them, so I started a Master’s in Artificial Intelligence at UMPSA while working. I finished with a CGPA of 3.76 and a thesis on efficient duplicate-question detection, spoke as a Google Speaker at AI Build 2025 and made the Top 20 of AWS National 2025 for training large language models.

chapters.title: Building the foundations
body: At AEM Energy Solutions the models only work if the data underneath them does, so I build the pipelines, the platforms and the AI tooling for the energy sector. The problems there led to QualityPlus: a tool that scores data quality and turns the failures into a review workflow instead of a spreadsheet.

chapters.title: Same curiosity, different tracks
body: Outside the day job I build to find out: LeadSightz in a weekend at the Cursor × Anthropic hackathon, Balang as a party game about probability, and Sepang Vision Lab, a digital twin that started as a question about how far public race data can go. Some ship, some don’t. Each one teaches me something the next one needs.

outro: Input → process → iterate → progress. Still iterating.

principles.title: Input
principles.detail: Start from the real question and the data that actually exists, not the data I wish existed.

principles.title: Process
principles.detail: Build the smallest system that answers it end to end, then make each layer solid before adding the next.

principles.title: Iterate
principles.detail: Measure against a baseline. If the clever version doesn't beat the simple one, say so and try again.

principles.title: Progress
principles.detail: Ship, write down what I learned, and carry it into the next project. Or the next run.

title: The work matters.
So does everything around it.
body: Outside work I run road races. It’s the same loop as engineering: show up, measure, adjust, repeat. Progress you only notice over months.
The rest happens around people: hackathons, industry demos, conferences, and the odd stage.
